questions.q: According to the lesson, which field in your run log is your best quality signal?
options: Tokens used and how long the run took
The prompt version that handled the run
The run ID and the time the run started
Whether a person approved, edited or rejected it
questions.explain: The lesson calls the human outcome, approved, edited or rejected, your best quality signal, which is why it belongs in every run's log entry.

questions.q: Your lead-routing automation has logged zero runs since yesterday morning, with no errors recorded. What's the most likely problem the lesson warns about?
options: The prompt cache expired, so new runs are being skipped
The effort level is set too low for the model to respond
A broken trigger, the most dangerous silent failure
The run log is full and has stopped recording new runs
questions.explain: A sudden drop in volume to zero usually means a broken trigger, which the lesson calls the most dangerous silent failure, so set an alert for no runs when you'd expect some.

questions.q: You want to cut costs on a high-volume email classification step. Which approach follows the lesson's advice?
options: Raise the effort level so the model gets each category right the first time
Use low effort or a smaller model, then confirm quality with your golden set
Send the full customer record so the model needs fewer follow-up calls
Put the changing email first and the stable instructions last to help caching
questions.explain: The lesson recommends low effort for classification and testing a smaller model against your golden set; it also says to trim context and put stable content first for caching.
